opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the most interesting questions in multilingual work, and honestly I think the answer is more nuanced than the early optimism suggested.

The basic intuition is that languages share a lot of structure. There's shared syntax across language families, shared scripts, cognates, borrowed vocabulary, and at a deeper level a lot of shared semantics, because people everywhere are talking about similar things in the world. So when you train jointly, the model can learn representations that aren't tied to one language, and lower-resource languages in particular can benefit from the structure learned from higher-resource ones. That's the positive transfer story, and we do see it, especially for related languages and for languages where you just don't have much data on their own.

But there's another side to it, which people often call the curse of multilinguality. You have a fixed capacity budget, and as you add more languages, they start competing for it. At some point the gains from sharing are outweighed by interference, and you see performance on individual languages, sometimes even the high-resource ones, start to degrade. So it isn't a free lunch. The question becomes how you balance it: how much capacity, what data mixture, how you sample across languages.

Something we've thought about a lot at Cohere For AI, particularly with the Aya work, is that the data itself matters enormously. A lot of what looks like transfer, or the lack of it, is really about data quality and coverage. If your data for a language is mostly machine-translated, or scraped and noisy, you're transferring artifacts as much as knowledge. So part of the work was building human-curated data across a large number of languages, so we could actually see what joint training buys you when the signal is good.

There's also a subtler issue around what transfers. Some capabilities, like reasoning patterns or instruction-following behavior, transfer surprisingly well across languages. Others, like cultural knowledge or safety behavior, often don't. We've seen models that are well aligned in English but much less robust in other languages, which tells you that some of these properties don't automatically generalize just because the model is multilingual. You have to be intentional about it.

So I'd frame it this way: joint training gives you a real opportunity for transfer, especially for languages that would otherwise be left behind, but you have to manage the trade-offs deliberately through data, capacity, and evaluation, rather than assume scale will take care of it.

r001.rationale: It says lower-resource languages can benefit and that high-resource performance can degrade, but does not state that the benefit comes at a small cost to high-resource languages.

r002.rationale: It attributes transfer partly to shared semantics across languages, which lets models learn representations not tied to one language.

r003.rationale: It discusses adding languages in joint training, but does not connect the number of pretraining languages to transfer during fine-tuning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's actually one of the more surprising and, honestly, still underexplained phenomena in the field. When you train a model jointly across many languages, you consistently see that lower-resource languages benefit from being trained alongside higher-resource ones. The question is really why, and what the mechanism is.

The way I tend to think about it is that languages aren't nearly as independent as we treat them. There's a huge amount of shared structure, whether that's at the level of syntax, of concepts, of the world knowledge that's being encoded. So when you train on a lot of English, or a lot of Spanish, you're not just learning English or Spanish. You're learning a representation of the world that happens to be expressed in that language. And when a lower-resource language comes along, it can essentially piggyback on that shared representation rather than having to learn everything from scratch with far less data.

Where it gets interesting is that the transfer is very uneven. It's not a uniform benefit. Languages that share scripts, or that are typologically close, or that have a lot of overlapping vocabulary through borrowing, tend to see much larger gains. And then you have languages that are really isolated in the training mix, where the tokenizer fragments them badly, where there's very little shared signal, and those often see much weaker transfer. So part of the work we did at Cohere For AI with Aya was really trying to understand that, because if you just assume transfer is free, you end up with models that look multilingual on a leaderboard but are actually quite brittle for the languages that need it most.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's a tension. It's sometimes called the curse of multilinguality, where as you add more languages to a fixed capacity model, you start to see interference. The high-resource languages can degrade, and you get competition for capacity. So the transfer benefits are real, but they're not unconditional. They depend on capacity, on the data mixture, on how you weight languages during training, and on the tokenizer, which I think is one of the most underappreciated levers in all of this. A lot of what looks like a language being hard is actually the tokenizer making it hard.

So my honest answer is that I understand transfer as this interplay between shared structure that the model can exploit and the constraints you've imposed on it through architecture and data choices. And I think we're still very early in being able to predict, for a given language, how much it's going to benefit. That's actually one of the open research questions I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: It says low-resource languages benefit, while high-resource languages can degrade as more languages compete for capacity. It does not characterize that cost as small.

r002.rationale: It attributes transfer to shared structure across languages, including concepts and a shared representation of the world.

r003.rationale: It discusses how adding languages affects interference in a fixed-capacity model, but does not connect the number of pretraining languages to transfer during fine-tuning.

astra-6.text:
I think the intuition is that languages share structure, so learning from one language can help the model learn another. When you train them jointly, you give the model an opportunity to learn representations that capture some of that shared structure, rather than having to learn everything independently for each language.

That’s particularly appealing for languages where you have very little training data. There’s the possibility of benefiting from the much larger amount of data available in other languages. But I’d be careful about treating that transfer as automatic. Languages can also compete for model capacity, and the balance of the training data matters. You can have an improvement on average while some languages actually get worse.

So the interesting question is: who benefits from sharing, and under what conditions? Are we improving performance for the languages with the least data, or are most of the gains going to languages that were already well represented? That’s where looking beyond a single aggregate measure becomes really important.

r001.rationale: It says low-data languages may benefit and that some languages may worsen, but does not specify a small cost to high-resource languages.

r002.rationale: It attributes transfer to shared structure generally, without identifying that structure as semantic.

r003.rationale: It does not raise how the number of languages in pretraining affects transfer during fine-tuning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as an opportunity for languages to share statistical strength. If you train a model jointly across languages, some of what it learns from a language with a lot of data can be useful for a language where data is scarce. The model doesn’t have to learn everything independently for every language.

But I think we have to be careful about treating that transfer as automatic. Languages differ, the amount of data available differs enormously, and the model has finite capacity. So you can have positive transfer, but you can also have interference, where improving performance on one language comes at the expense of another.

For me, the interesting question is: who actually benefits from sharing? An improvement in average performance doesn’t necessarily mean that the languages with the least data are better served. You have to look at performance language by language to understand whether joint training is delivering the benefit you hoped for.

r001.rationale: It says high-data languages can help data-scarce languages, but does not state that this may come at a small cost to high-resource languages.

r002.rationale: It describes sharing statistical strength across languages, but does not attribute transfer to shared semantic structures.

r003.rationale: It discusses language data, model capacity, and interference, but does not ask how the number of pretraining languages affects transfer during fine-tuning.
